title: Tissues, Organs and Systems
seo_title: Grade 10 Science (SNC2D): Tissues, Organs and Systems Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: Specialized cells and the four types of animal tissue; organs and organ systems (digestive, respiratory, circulatory) and how they interact; plant tissues, organs and systems; and medical technologies. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 9 and 10: Science (2008), Science, Grade 10, Academic (SNC2D), Strand B: Tissues, Organs, and Systems of Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Science (SNC2D) worksheets on tissues, organs and systems: specialized cells, levels of organization, the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems, and plant tissues. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
key_sub: Organ systems work together to keep the body alive.
body_html:
How to think about it

Cells with the same job form a tissue. Animals have four tissue types: epithelial (covers), connective (supports, such as bone and blood), muscle (moves) and nerve (signals). Tissues form organs such as the stomach, and organs work together in systems.

The digestive system breaks food down and absorbs nutrients; the respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide; the circulatory system carries them around the body. Plants have dermal, ground and vascular tissue; their organs are roots, stems, leaves and flowers, organized into the root system and the shoot system.

Example

Put in order: organ, cell, organ system, tissue.

Smallest first

Answer: cell, tissue, organ, organ system

Example

Which two systems work together to get oxygen to the muscles?

One takes in oxygen, one carries it.

Answer: respiratory and circulatory

Common mistakes

  • Calling blood an organ: it is a connective tissue.
  • Thinking organ systems work alone.
  • Saying plants have no tissues.

faq.q: Why are red blood cells specialized?
faq.a: They have no nucleus and are full of hemoglobin, so they carry as much oxygen as possible.
It carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves.

items.q: At which level of organization is palisade mesophyll?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: At which level of organization is a red blood cell?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a guard cell?
items.e: A guard cell has a thicker inner wall: a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma.

items.q: A root hair cell has a long, narrow extension. How does this help it?
c: energy to swim to the egg
many proteins made and packaged for secretion
a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts
an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which cells of the neural tissue support and protect neurons?
items.e: They make up more than half the volume of neural tissue.

items.q: At which level of organization is the heart?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which cell has a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body, giving many proteins made and packaged for secretion?
c: a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes
items.e: Each specialized cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: At which level of organization is a leaf?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: How does a frog breathe in water?
c: it does not breathe in water
items.e: On land it also uses its lungs and buccal cavity.

items.q: Which cell has a tail (flagellum) and many mitochondria, giving energy to swim to the egg?
items.e: Each specialized cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: At which level of organization is epithelium?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which cell has many chloroplasts, giving more light absorbed for photosynthesis?
items.e: Each specialized cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: What does a male frog have that a female does not?
c: vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimb
items.e: These help the male call and hold the female.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a xylem vessel?
c: no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls
items.e: A xylem vessel has no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls: an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support.

items.q: At which level of organization is the circulatory system?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which muscle is involuntary and striated?
items.e: It has intercalated discs.

items.q: Which cell has a thicker inner wall, giving a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma?
items.e: Each specialized cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: Where is ciliated epithelium found, or what does it do?
c: the lining of the stomach and intestine, with tall cells
the dry surface of the skin, the moist lining of the mouth and pharynx
items.e: Ciliated epithelium: the bronchioles and fallopian tubes.

items.q: Why is the frog called cold-blooded?
c: its body temperature changes with the environment (poikilothermic)
items.e: It goes into winter sleep (hibernation).

items.q: Which cell has a long, narrow extension, giving a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts?
items.e: Each specialized cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for breathing faster when you run?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for moving nutrients from food to cells?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Noah asks: what is the main job of the excretory system?
c: It removes wastes from the body.
It moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It collects information and sends messages that control the body.
It takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.
items.e: The excretory system removes wastes from the body.

items.q: What level is made of many tissues working together?
items.e: Many tissues make up an organ.

items.q: Which level of organization is the lining of the stomach?
items.e: The lining of the stomach is a tissue.

items.q: Which level of organization is cardiac muscle?
items.e: Cardiac muscle is a tissue.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for removing wastes from the blood?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Which level of organization is xylem?
items.e: Xylem is a tissue.

items.q: Which level of organization is the digestive system?
items.e: The digestive system is an organ system.

items.q: Which organ system does the spinal cord belong to?
items.e: The spinal cord is part of the nervous system.

items.q: Which organ system does the heart belong to?
items.e: The heart is part of the circulatory system.

items.q: Which level is the largest?
items.e: An organism is made of all its systems.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for pulling your hand away from a hot stove?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Which level of organization is a red blood cell?
items.e: A red blood cell is a cell.

items.q: Which organ system does the diaphragm belong to?
items.e: The diaphragm is part of the respiratory system.

items.q: Which list goes from smallest to largest?
c: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
cell → organ → tissue → organ system → organism
tissue → cell → organ → organ system → organism
cell → tissue → organ system → organ → organism
items.e: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems.

items.q: Nathan asks: what is the main job of the digestive system?
c: It moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.
It supports the body and protects organs.
It removes wastes from the body.
items.e: The digestive system breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.

items.q: Which organ system does the femur belong to?
items.e: The femur is part of the skeletal system.

items.q: Which organ system does the skin belong to?
items.e: The skin is part of the integumentary system.

items.q: Leah asks: what is the main job of the muscular system?
c: It collects information and sends messages that control the body.
It removes wastes from the body.
It moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It moves the body by pulling on bones.
items.e: The muscular system moves the body by pulling on bones.

items.q: Where does air come from just before it reaches a bronchus?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: What is the job of the alveoli?
c: Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.
Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which food molecule does lipase break down?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: Protease in the small intestine breaks proteins into amino acids. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: Where does air come from just before it reaches a bronchiole?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through a bronchus. Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: Carbohydrase from the pancreas breaks starch into sugars. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: What does lipase break lipids (fats and oils) down into?
items.e: Big molecules are broken into small ones that can be absorbed.

items.q: What is the job of the intercostal muscles?
c: Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
Bones that protect the lungs and heart.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system does this? It moves food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis.
items.e: The esophagus (esophagus): It moves food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis.

items.q: Which food molecule does amylase break down?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system does this? It stores feces before they are removed from the body.
items.e: The rectum: It stores feces before they are removed from the body.

items.q: What is the main job of the gall bladder?
c: It absorbs water and mineral salts from undigested food.
It stores bile until it is needed in the small intestine.
It churns food and makes gastric juice with protease and acid to start digesting proteins.
It moves food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis.
items.e: The gall bladder: It stores bile until it is needed in the small intestine.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through the trachea (windpipe). Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: The tongue rolls chewed food into a ball. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: The stomach walls churn food. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: What is the main job of the mouth?
c: Teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts to digest starch.
It makes pancreatic juice with carbohydrase, protease and lipase.
It makes bile, which breaks fats into small droplets.
It completes digestion and absorbs digested food into the blood.
items.e: The mouth: Teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts to digest starch.

items.q: What does protease break proteins down into?
items.e: Big molecules are broken into small ones that can be absorbed.

items.q: Which blood vessel has a thick, muscular, elastic wall to withstand high pressure?
items.e: An artery has a thick, muscular, elastic wall to withstand high pressure.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the aorta to the kidney?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: A student counts 12 pulse beats in 10 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 12 × (60 ÷ 10).

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood to the muscle of the heart wall?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Blood enters the pulmonary artery. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Blood enters the right ventricle. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells?
items.e: A capillary carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.

items.q: Which blood vessel has a wall only one cell thick?
items.e: A capillary has a wall only one cell thick.

items.q: Does the pulmonary artery carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

items.q: Blood is in the left ventricle. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Blood is in the lungs. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 75 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 75 mL. What is the cardiac output in L per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 75 × 75 = 5625 mL/min.

items.q: A student counts 36 pulse beats in 20 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 36 × (60 ÷ 20).

items.q: Does the vena cava carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The vena cava carries deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.

items.q: A student counts 14 pulse beats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 14 × (60 ÷ 15).

items.q: Blood is in the pulmonary artery. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Does the pulmonary vein carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. What is the cardiac output in L per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 70 × 70 = 4900 mL/min.

items.q: What does a vein do?
c: It carries blood away from the heart.
It carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.
It carries blood back to the heart.
items.e: A vein carries blood back to the heart.

items.q: Palisade cells are near the top of the leaf. How does this help the leaf?
c: Gases can move easily between the cells.
They have a large surface area to absorb light.
Carbon dioxide only has a short distance to diffuse to the cells.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Mineral salts absorbed by the roots reach the leaves. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: What is heartwood?
c: the dark central wood made of dead xylem filled with tannins and resins
items.e: It is durable and no longer conducts water.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf?
items.e: Spongy parenchyma: loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf.

items.q: Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts. How does this help the leaf?
c: Gases can move easily between the cells.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
Carbon dioxide can diffuse in and oxygen can diffuse out.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: The upper surface has a waxy layer. How does this help the leaf?
c: They have a large surface area to absorb light.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: The spongy layer has air spaces. How does this help the leaf?
c: Gases can move easily between the cells.
They have a large surface area to absorb light.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Sugars move from the leaves to the growing shoot tip. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Which tissue transports water and mineral ions in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: Which tissue transports sucrose in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as cells that open and close the stomatal pore?
items.e: Guard cells: cells that open and close the stomatal pore.

items.q: A rose in blue-coloured water develops blue streaks in its petals. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Leaves are thin. How does this help the leaf?
c: Carbon dioxide only has a short distance to diffuse to the cells.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Guard cells surround each stoma. How does this help the leaf?
c: They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
They open and close the stoma to control water loss.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Leaves have veins (xylem and phloem). How does this help the leaf?
c: They bring water and carry away sugars.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
They open and close the stoma to control water loss.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Red dye rises up a celery stalk placed in red-coloured water. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: The lower surface has many stomata. How does this help the leaf?
c: They have a large surface area to absorb light.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
Carbon dioxide can diffuse in and oxygen can diffuse out.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Which tissue transports amino acids in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: Water moves up from the roots to the leaves of a balsam plant. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: A ring of bark is removed from a tree and the bark above the ring swells with sugar. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.
